prompt: Which kind of quality may the business legitimately trade for time, by the lesson?
hint: One of them is really a question of scope.

choices.text: Internal quality, such as fewer tests in code nobody sees
choices.why: That is the trade the lesson argues against: it makes every next change slower, and the payoff line comes within weeks.

choices.text: External quality, such as a plainer first screen
choices.why: Right: a plainer screen or fewer options in a first version is a smaller scope, which the business is entitled to choose.

choices.text: Neither, because quality is fixed by policy at Carreto
choices.why: The lesson does not fix quality by policy; the next section sets a different bar for different parts.

choices.text: Both, provided the debt is written down afterwards
choices.why: Writing debt down keeps it prudent, but it does not turn internal quality into a free corner.

prompt: In Fowler's design stamina graph, what happens after the design payoff line?
hint: One line keeps its slope and the other bends.

choices.text: The skimping project falls further behind each week
choices.why: Right: the no-design line has bent flatter, so each feature costs it more, while the good-design line keeps its slope.

choices.text: The two lines run together, so design stops mattering
choices.why: They cross at the line and then separate; that crossing is the whole point.

choices.text: The no-design project catches up once its debt is repaid
choices.why: The graph shows no repayment; it shows what happens when the design is not kept healthy.

choices.text: Both projects slow down at the same rate
choices.why: The good-design line keeps its slope. Only the no-design line bends.

prompt: Why did Fowler call design stamina a hypothesis rather than a finding?
hint: What would proving it require?

choices.text: He drew it before he had worked on a large project
choices.why: Fowler had decades of experience by 2007; the reason is about measurement.

choices.text: It contradicts the project triangle, which is a proven model
choices.why: The triangle is a planning picture, not a proven model, and the two do not contradict each other.

choices.text: Productivity cannot be measured well enough to prove it
choices.why: Right: it rests on the experience of people who have worked on both kinds of code.

choices.text: It holds for small teams and he was unsure about big ones
choices.why: Team size is not the qualification the lesson gives.

prompt: With n(n − 1) / 2 paths of communication among n people, how many pairs have to keep in step in a team of 8?
hint: 8 times 7, halved.

prompt: Multi-stop loads: 6 weeks with tests, or 4 weeks as a special case. The next two Pricing features would each take 2 to 3 weeks longer on the special case. At the low end of that estimate, when are the two saved weeks gone?
hint: Compare the saving with the first extra cost.

choices.text: Never: two weeks saved are two weeks saved
choices.why: That ignores the extra cost the special case adds to every later change in the same code.

choices.text: After both features, which together cost the two weeks
choices.why: Each feature costs at least 2 weeks more, so the first alone cancels the saving.

choices.text: Only if the special-cased code has bugs in production
choices.why: The cost the team estimated is slower change, with or without bugs.

choices.text: With the first of the two features
choices.why: Right: 2 extra weeks on the first feature cancel the 2 saved, and the second feature is pure loss.

prompt: Why does adding people to a late project rarely give the time back, by Brooks's argument?
hint: Two costs arrive with every new person.

choices.text: Newcomers need training, and coordination grows
choices.why: Right: newcomers learn from the people already doing the work, which slows them, and the paths of communication grow faster than the team.

choices.text: New people write lower-quality code than the original team
choices.why: Brooks's argument is about learning and coordination, not about the skill of the newcomers.

choices.text: Budgets do not allow hiring in the middle of a project
choices.why: The law holds even when money is available; it is about how work is shared.

choices.text: Managers hide the delay until it is too late to hire
choices.why: A real problem in some places, but not Brooks's reason.

prompt: What sets the quality bar for a piece of work, by the lesson?
hint: Three things about the work, none of them about the team.

choices.text: How important the owning team feels the work is
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: the quote engine is unglamorous and deserves a high bar.

choices.text: One company-wide standard, the same for every part
choices.why: A single dial is what both slogans assume, and what the lesson rejects.

choices.text: Its lifetime, its rate of change, and what being wrong costs
choices.why: Right: the code that pays drivers and a script that runs once deserve different bars.

choices.text: Whatever the most senior engineer prefers
choices.why: Preference is what the table of bars replaced, ending the arguments about gold-plating.

prompt: Match each kind of work at Carreto to the bar Renata set for it.
hint: Consequence and lifetime decide.

pairs.right: a reviewed design and tests on every money path
tried on a copy of production, then deleted
a second person checks the totals

right_distractors: a run in the tax authority's test environment

prompt: A one-off migration moves a million rows. Why does it still get a light bar?
hint: How is its risk handled?

choices.text: Large migrations rarely fail, so testing them in advance adds little
choices.why: The lesson makes no such claim; the migration is rehearsed precisely because it is risky.

choices.text: Its risk is handled by rehearsal, not by building it to last
choices.why: Right: it runs once, so engineering it for a long life buys nothing; the rehearsal is where the care goes.

choices.text: Migrations belong to Platform, which sets its own rules
choices.why: Ownership is not the reason. The bar follows consequence and lifetime.

choices.text: Being wrong costs nothing, since the data can be restored
choices.why: Being wrong costs a rerun, which is cheap only because the run was rehearsed on a copy first.

prompt: A team says: "We don't have time for design on this one; we'll sort it out later." Nobody writes anything down. Where does this sit in Fowler's quadrant, and what does the lesson ask for?
hint: Two questions: on purpose or not, prudent or not.

choices.text: Inadvertent and prudent; nothing needs to be done
choices.why: The team chose the shortcut knowingly, so it is not inadvertent.

choices.text: Deliberate and prudent, since the team knows it is borrowing
choices.why: Knowing is not enough; without a reason, an owner and a date there is no plan to repay, which makes it reckless.

choices.text: Inadvertent and reckless, the result of not knowing better
choices.why: The team knows better and is choosing not to; the debt is deliberate.

choices.text: Deliberate and reckless; agree only once it is prudent and written down
choices.why: Right: the only debt to agree to is deliberate and prudent, and deliberate means written down with an owner, a reason and a date.

prompt: With the new CT-e layout's date fixed and the three engineers who know the code fixed too, which corner of the triangle moved?
hint: Two corners were pinned.

choices.text: Time, by asking the tax authority for an extension
choices.why: The date belonged to the tax authority and was not negotiable.

choices.text: Cost, by bringing in engineers from Matching
choices.why: People who do not know the tax rules would have slowed the three down, which is Brooks's law.

choices.text: Internal quality, by skipping tests on the new fields
choices.why: The first two rows kept the full bar, tests against the tax authority's validation included.

choices.text: Scope
choices.why: Right: everything not needed for every common CT-e to be authorised on the day was moved after it.

prompt: Which items of the CT-e work had to be finished by the date? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask of each: what happens on the day if it is not done?

choices.text: The new mandatory fields for road freight
choices.why: Yes: without them about 97% of Carreto's CT-es are rejected.

choices.text: Multimodal and the other rare cases
choices.why: About 3% of CT-es, issued through a manual procedure for a few weeks.

choices.text: The new validation rules
choices.why: Yes: without them CT-es are rejected one truck at a time.

choices.text: The back-office screen that corrects a CT-e after issue
choices.why: An engineer made the few corrections a week until it shipped a month later.

choices.text: Restructuring the generator around versioned layouts
choices.why: Nothing happens on the day without it; it is where the three options differ.

prompt: Who decides the trade between quality, time and cost, by the lesson?
hint: The architect has a different job in it.

choices.text: The architect, who understands the engineering
choices.why: That is one of the two habits the lesson names. The architect recommends; the owners of time and money decide.

choices.text: The team that will build it, since it is the one that carries the consequences
choices.why: The team informs the options, but the trade spends the company's time and money.

choices.text: The business, with the consequences made explicit by the architect
choices.why: Right: the architect's job is to make each choice's consequences plain enough for an informed decision, and to write down what was agreed.

choices.text: Whoever owns the date
choices.why: For the CT-e the date's owner was the tax authority, which decided nothing about Carreto's options.

prompt: Option A takes 12 engineer-weeks, and Carreto plans with R$ 6,500 per engineer-week. What does option A cost, in reais?
hint: Engineer-weeks times the weekly cost.

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend presenting three options rather than one?
hint: What does a single option ask of the decider?

choices.text: One option asks for approval; three give a real choice
choices.why: Right: with one option the decider learns nothing about what else was possible, and two invite splitting the difference.

choices.text: Three fit on one slide, which executives prefer
choices.why: Format is not the argument; the argument is about what the decider learns.

choices.text: Three lets the architect hide the preferred one in the middle
choices.why: Renata states her recommendation openly; the options are not a trick.

choices.text: Regulation requires three quotes for any spending
choices.why: No rule in the lesson asks for three; the reason is the quality of the decision.

prompt: Options B and C cost the same in total, R$ 175,500. What does choosing C buy Carreto?
hint: Look at where the risky work sits on the calendar.

choices.text: A saving, because the patch is cheaper than the rebuild
choices.why: The totals are equal; the patch is followed by the rebuild.

choices.text: A better generator than B produces at the end
choices.why: C ends with the same generator as B, a quarter later.

choices.text: Margin: the risky rebuild moves away from the fixed date
choices.why: Right: six weeks of margin instead of one, paid for by carrying the patch for a quarter.

choices.text: Freedom to skip the rebuild if the quarter is busy
choices.why: That is the risk Sílvio named, and the reason Renata made the rebuild a condition of recommending C.

prompt: Which line of Renata's one-page note was the one Helena needed most?
hint: Helena owns product priorities.

choices.text: Why the tax authority's date cannot move
choices.why: Important context, but it did not decide anything for Helena.

choices.text: What each option takes from her roadmap
choices.why: Right: B took the three CT-e engineers for nine weeks, A or C for four, and the same people were due on return loads.

choices.text: The arithmetic of the loaded cost per week
choices.why: That line was Sílvio's concern more than Helena's.

choices.text: Which option the engineers preferred
choices.why: The note did not argue for the engineers' preference; it laid out consequences.

prompt: The last line of Renata's debt entry, "___ if", names the event that would make the interest jump, such as a new layout announced before repayment.
hint: It tells a future reader when to look at the decision again.

prompt: Put the five things Renata's one-page note said in the order she wrote them.
hint: From the constraint, through the choice, to what it costs the roadmap.
items: The date, and why it cannot move
The scope handled by hand for a few weeks
What each option takes from the roadmap
trap: Putting the recommendation first turns the note into a request for approval, which is what three options exist to avoid.

prompt: Helena wants a dashboard for shippers to show at a trade fair in two weeks; afterwards the real one will be built from scratch. The team proposes skipping tests. What fits the lesson?
hint: Where does this code's life end relative to the payoff line?

choices.text: Refuse: internal quality is not the free corner
choices.why: That holds for code that will be changed again. This code's life ends before the payoff line.

choices.text: Fair, and it is a good moment to skip the review too
choices.why: The bar is light, but the lesson does not argue for removing every check.

choices.text: Fair, provided it is truly thrown away after the fair
choices.why: Right: cutting corners pays for work that dies before the line, like a demonstration. The risk is the demo that quietly becomes the product.

choices.text: Refuse unless the business signs a debt register entry
choices.why: A throwaway carries no debt if it is thrown away; the register is for code that stays.

prompt: Sílvio asked whether the fifteen engineer-weeks would really happen next quarter. What made option C acceptable to Renata?
hint: Her answer was a condition.

choices.text: Bruno promised to find the time himself
choices.why: A promise is not a plan. Renata asked for something more durable.

choices.text: Sílvio approving a larger budget for Payments
choices.why: The total cost was already the same as B; budget was not the issue.

choices.text: An agreement that the patch would never be touched
choices.why: Freezing the patch would not repay anything, and the next layout would still come.

choices.text: The repayment on the roadmap, with owner and date
choices.why: Right: "it goes on the roadmap now, with an owner and a date, or I recommend B".

prompt: Option C costs R$ 78,000 now, plus 15 engineer-weeks next quarter at R$ 6,500 each. What is its total cost, in reais?
hint: Price the later work, then add.
